Six defects. Every one passed a test.
Read the table, not the verdict.

A short note on what two adversarial audits found in work we had already signed off, and the one mechanism behind all of it.

Boulder Research 10 November 2026 Method ~1 min read
Contents
  1. What the audits found
  2. The mechanism

We signed off a piece of work as complete. Then we asked a second reviewer to refute the same claim instead of confirming it.

Same evidence. Different question. It found six defects.

What the audits found

  • A gate that computed its verdict from position alone. Its own table showed a velocity divergence; its verdict line said "match".
  • An orphan check that passed because the fields it should have flagged were exempt by construction.
  • A goal that said "every field" when the tool compared 30 of 77.
  • A negative control that the fix it guarded quietly absorbed.
  • A throughput "gate" that parsed a document and measured nothing.

Every one of them had passed a test.

The mechanism

The test and the claim came from the same process, and the process checked that the test passed, not that the test measured the claim.

Ask a separate party to refute the claim, not confirm it.

The remedy is structural:

  1. Ask someone else to break the claim.
  2. Read the table instead of the verdict line.
  3. Keep every number attached to the condition it holds under.

That's why our published numbers read like "bit-identical over 23,820 ticks, on 30 of the 77 fields" rather than something rounder.
